parts:
The review is saved as `papers/weil-depth/REVIEW_CLAUDE_20260909.md` in your repo (with my verification scripts under `numerics/review_claude/`) and in the RH3 project. The short version:

**Accuracy.** I found no error. I checked every proof by hand and independently recomputed the key objects by routes that share nothing with the package: the form in eq. (2.6) agrees with $\sum_\rho|\hat f_c(\gamma_\rho)|^2$ over actual zeta zeros to $6\times10^{-10}$, the head matrix agrees with a Fourier-side evaluation to $10^{-11}$, the full-output Grams agree with direct quadrature to 20+ digits, and all analytic constants reproduce to every displayed digit. Both builders, the independent implementation, the analyzer and the review checks reproduce the archived certificates exactly in a third environment. The only soft spots are two functional-analytic passages (Prop. 3.3 and the closure step in Prop. 4.2) written at sketch level; a human should write those out fully.

**What the numbers really are.** The floors $10^{-26}$ and $10^{-34}$ are round targets. The same matrices certify $3.3\times10^{-23}$ and $1.3\times10^{-28}$, and a ball Rayleigh quotient of the head ground state gives rigorous upper bounds $4.14\times10^{-23}$ and $6.8\times10^{-28}$, so you have two-sided enclosures with gaps of ×1.2 and ×5. Running your unmodified builder at $\log2,\dots,\log6$ gives a certified profile of $\lambda_{\min}(L)$ from $1.3\times10^{-3}$ down to $6.8\times10^{-28}$; the $\log5$ row reproduces Zhu's lower bound at length 1.6 ($8.9\times10^{-18}$) by a completely different reduction, which is a nice cross-validation between the two programs. The ground state is even and simple at every horizon, with a geometric eigenvalue ladder of ratio $\sim10^{5.5}$.

**Interest.** A competent, unusually well-engineered certificate that extends the rigorously certified window from 1.6 to $\log7$ (first with the prime 5 and the composite 6), and Lemma 4.1 is a genuinely nice tool — but it is a finite statement in a small niche, not a conceptual advance, and the paper mostly knows it. The scalar tail floor shows the same doubly-exponential wall Zhu describes: keeping the floor at ~0.6 needs $N\approx310$ at $\log8$, $950$ at $\log11$, $4400$ at $\log16$, $27{,}000$ as $L\to3$, so the method caps out around $L\approx2.7$. §7's storage/recursion material is correct algebra but points at no mechanism; I'd trim it.

**Top suggestions.** Report the sharpened two-sided floors and the profile table; rewrite "Relation to earlier work" (positivity through $\log 2$ is classical — Yoshida, Connes–Consani — and Zhu's two-sided bounds and impossibility argument deserve engagement); consolidate the theorems around $\log 7$; write out Prop. 3.3; add per-sector enclosures; fix the small items (grammar, undefined "second slab", environment inconsistency). Next steps in order: the cheap enclosure/profile additions, then $\log 8$ at $N=512$, then — if you want to change the scaling rather than add a horizon — a structured (band-limited) tail bound; and this paper is the most natural entry point for a Lean collaborator.

Sources: [Zhu, arXiv:2608.24827](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24827), [Connes–Consani, arXiv:2006.13771](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.13771)

parts:
Yes — and for this repository it's not really optional going forward: the next experiment ($\log 8$ at $N=512$) will produce a matrix archive around 250 MB, which is over GitHub's hard 100 MB per-file limit for ordinary git. So the choice is LFS or keeping the archives out of the tree entirely, and now is the cheapest moment to decide.

Where you stand: the working tree is 125 MB, essentially all of it the ten `*.json.gz` ball-matrix archives plus the v0.1 ZIP (everything else across all six papers is under 4 MB). The `.git` directory is already 153 MB, because today's round replaced two archives and gzip data doesn't delta-compress, so history now holds both versions — that will happen on every review round that rebuilds a certificate. GitHub's current LFS terms are generous: Free and Pro personal accounts get 10 GiB of storage and 10 GiB of bandwidth per month, the old data packs are gone in favour of metered overage, and only downloads count (against your quota, not the downloader's). At today's size that's roughly eighty full clones a month before you'd pay anything, and people who only want the papers can clone with `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1` and pull no matrices at all.

What I'd do, concretely, on your Mac (needs `brew install git-lfs`):

```bash
git lfs install
git lfs migrate import --everything --include="*.json.gz,*.zip"
git lfs ls-files | head          # should list the archives and the v0.1 ZIP
git push --force --all origin    # history is rewritten; fine while nobody else has cloned
```

That leaves `.gitattributes` tracking `*.json.gz` and `*.zip`, shrinks the git history to a few MB, and moves the 146 MB of existing large blobs into LFS storage. Everything else (source, PDFs, certificates with their archive hashes, enclosures, scripts) stays in plain git.

Two caveats worth knowing. First, anyone who clones without git-lfs installed silently gets 130-byte pointer files where the archives should be, and `certify_arb.py --reuse` would then die with an obscure gzip error — I'd add a one-line pointer-file check to the replay and enclosure scripts and a sentence to `numerics/README.md`; I can do that now if you like. Second, Zenodo's GitHub integration snapshots GitHub's auto-generated source tarball, which contains the pointer files, not the LFS content. Given your stated deposit scope (preprint only, code and archives on request) that doesn't bite, but if you ever want a DOI'd copy of the matrices themselves, upload them to the Zenodo record manually rather than relying on the integration.

The alternative — not versioning the archives at all and treating them as deterministic derived data (all seven rebuild in about eight minutes; the certificate JSONs already carry pivots and hashes) — is defensible, but it gives up the "replay from the saved balls without rebuilding" property the package was designed around. I'd keep them, in LFS.

Sources: [GitHub Docs — Git LFS billing](https://docs.github.com/billing/managing-billing-for-git-large-file-storage/about-billing-for-git-large-file-storage), [GitHub community — LFS metered billing FAQ](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/61362)

metadata.source: Claude Cowork session event, completed public message

parts:
Short version: it wouldn't compromise the mathematics, but Drive/Box are the wrong tool for this particular job, and the cheap-at-scale option you're looking for is Zenodo, not a consumer drive.

The reason it wouldn't compromise anything is that the proof-relevant content is already small and already in git: the certificate JSONs carry every pivot and the SHA-256 of the archive they were computed from, and the enclosures carry theirs. The archives themselves are derived data — deterministic output of `certify_arb.py` — whose only job is to let someone replay without rebuilding. So the design that keeps integrity is "hashes and pivots in git, big bytes anywhere, and a script that fetches an archive and refuses to use it unless the hash matches." Once you have that, the host is a transport decision, and you should pick it on longevity, friction and cost.

| | GitHub LFS | Google Drive / Box | Zenodo |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost at your scale | 10 GB storage + 10 GB/month download free, then \$0.07/GB-month and \$0.0875/GB downloaded | ~\$2/month for 100 GB (Google One), ~\$10/month for 2 TB; Box Pro similar | Free; 50 GB per record, unlimited records, +150 GB discretionary allowance |
| Versioning tied to the paper | Automatic (per commit) | None — a link points at whatever is there now | Per-version DOI plus a stable concept DOI; published files are immutable |
| Scripted download | `git lfs pull`; silent pointer files if git-lfs isn't installed | Fragile: virus-scan interstitials on files over 100 MB, "download quota exceeded" on popular files, permission changes | Plain HTTPS/REST, checksums displayed per file |
| Longevity / citability | As long as the GitHub account exists | Tied to a personal account and its sharing settings | CERN-backed archive built for exactly this; citable |
| Who pays for downloads | You, per GB after 10 GB/month | You, via the plan | Nobody |

Two things fall out of that. First, the cost argument doesn't favour Drive: at a few gigabytes LFS overage is a dollar or two a month, Drive is two to ten, and Zenodo is zero. Bandwidth is the only place LFS gets expensive — every reader who clones with LFS active downloads everything, charged to you — and that's exactly the scenario where an external data repository is better anyway. Second, using Drive would need the same manifest-plus-verify script you'd write for Zenodo, so it's equal effort with a worse host; the friction and impermanence would also read badly to the Lean and academic audience you want, for whom a DOI'd data record is the expected form.

What I'd actually do, in two stages. Now: LFS for the archives, because at 125 MB it is the least effort, and it solves the immediate problem that the $\log 8$ archive won't fit in plain git. At each version you archive on Zenodo (which you're already planning for the preprints): upload that version's matrix archives as files on the same record, and add a `numerics/ARCHIVES.json` manifest to git listing path, DOI/URL, size and SHA-256, plus a `fetch_archives.py` that downloads and verifies. At that point the LFS copies of old versions can be dropped if quota ever matters, and readers who want to replay get the files from a permanent place without costing you bandwidth. That is roughly how the large computer-assisted proofs handle their data, and it isn't overkill — the manifest and fetcher are perhaps forty lines, and I can write them and the pointer-file guard now if you'd like.

One unrelated caution while we're on storage: if macOS is syncing your `~/Documents` to iCloud Drive (the "Desktop & Documents Folders" option), the repository's `.git` directory is being synced by a file-sync client, which is a known way to get corrupted or evicted objects. Worth checking that it's off for that folder, or moving the clone somewhere unsynced.

Sources: [GitHub community — LFS metered billing FAQ](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/61362), [GitHub Docs — Git LFS billing](https://docs.github.com/billing/managing-billing-for-git-large-file-storage/about-billing-for-git-large-file-storage), [Zenodo — manage storage quota](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/deposit/manage-quota/), [Zenodo — size limitations](https://support.zenodo.org/help/en-gb/1-upload-deposit/80-what-are-the-size-limitations-of-zenodo)

Your reasoning is right, and the layout is favourable for the squash: `main` (e2d075f) contains no large blobs at all; every heavy file entered in the three commits on `finite-horizon-weil`, so a squash of a tree without them gives a clean `main`, and deleting the branch makes the blobs unreachable.

**What's on your machine now.** All ten large files (seven `central_matrices.json.gz`, two `independent_matrices.json.gz`, the v0.1 package ZIP — 122 MB) are in `papers/weil-depth/numerics-archives/`, mirroring their original paths, with a `README.md` and `SHA256SUMS.txt`. A new `papers/weil-depth/.gitignore` excludes that folder, any `*.json.gz` under `numerics/output/`, logs and LaTeX aux files, so regenerated archives can never be committed by accident. The tracked `weil-depth` tree is 3.5 MB with nothing over 1 MB. The v0.1 ZIP's small contents (tex, docs, code, 9/5 certificate) are extracted under `archive/drafts/v0.1_2026-09-09/package/` so that draft stays readable in git.

Two additions make the repository fully verifiable without the archives. Each certificate and enclosure now records `matrices_content_sha256`, a hash of the four ball matrices and run parameters that ignores timestamps and runtime metadata; I confirmed the original 9/5 build (Python 3.12) and $\log 7$ build (3.10) hash identically to my rebuilds under 3.11, so anyone can regenerate an archive and know it is the same object. And the scripts (`certify_arb.py --reuse`, `enclose_certificate.py`, `analyze_certificate.py`, `compare_implementations.py`) fall back to `$WEIL_ARCHIVES/<same relative path>` when a file is missing, with a clear error otherwise — so wherever you put the folder, one environment variable restores replay. The PDF, `SHA256SUMS.txt` (73 versioned files) and `BUILD_RECORD.json` are regenerated; README, STATUS, `numerics/README.md`, the archive index and Appendix C describe the arrangement.

**Git steps**, in order:

```bash
cd ~/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity
git add -A papers/weil-depth
git commit -m "weil-depth v0.3: ball archives moved out of git; content hashes; archive fallback"

git checkout main
git merge --squash finite-horizon-weil
git commit -m "Weil-depth paper v0.3 (squashed from finite-horizon-weil)"
git push origin main

git branch -D finite-horizon-weil
git push origin --delete finite-horizon-weil
git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now
```

Two cautions. Back up `numerics-archives/` somewhere else before the last two lines — after the branch is gone and gc runs, that folder is the only copy (regenerable, but eight minutes of compute you don't need to repeat). And GitHub keeps unreachable objects for a while: the repository's reported size may not drop immediately and the old commits remain fetchable by hash until GitHub's own gc runs (support will do it on request), which only matters if you care about the size figure.
